result: Both Nb39 and miniGsi biosensors are recruited to plasma membrane DOR upon agonist treatment (SNC80 and DPDPE), with concentration-dependent responses. miniGsi shows higher potency (EC50=2.284 nM) than Nb39 (EC50=22.7 nM) for SNC80. The sensors show differential recruitment patterns: DPDPE recruits Nb39 more strongly while SNC80 recruits miniGsi more strongly. MiniGs (Gs sensor) is not recruited, confirming specificity for Gi-coupled DOR.
evaluation: Claims C20-C30, C88-C89 are well-supported by TIR-FM imaging data in Figures 1B-G showing rapid, agonist-specific, concentration-dependent recruitment with appropriate controls (inverse agonist ICI, miniGs negative control). Statistical significance is demonstrated, EC50 values are quantified, and differential agonist effects are clearly documented.

result: In intracellular compartments, Nb39 is rapidly recruited to DOR upon SNC80 treatment (within 30s), while miniGsi is not recruited to intracellular DOR despite being recruited to PM DOR in the same cells. This differential recruitment suggests SNC80 promotes distinct active DOR conformations at different subcellular locations.
evaluation: Claims C32-C40 are strongly supported by confocal imaging data (Figures 1I-M, Videos 1-2) showing clear differential recruitment. The antagonist reversal experiment (C34, Figure 1-supplement 2) confirms specificity. Controls include miniGs negative control (C37) and demonstration that both sensors recruit to PM DOR in the same cells (C38-C39), ruling out expression or technical artifacts.

result: Nb39 recruitment to intracellular DOR requires direct activation of intracellular receptors by membrane-permeable agonist SNC80, not activation of PM DOR. The peptide agonist DPDPE (which doesn't cross membranes) fails to recruit Nb39 to intracellular DOR. Pharmacological blockade of PM DOR with ICI does not prevent Nb39 recruitment to intracellular DOR, and PTX treatment (inactivating endogenous Gαi/o) does not enable miniGsi recruitment.
evaluation: Claims C41-C49 are well-supported by experiments using membrane-impermeable antagonist ICI and peptide agonist DPDPE (Figures 1L, 2A-C). The logic is sound: DPDPE activates PM DOR but not IC DOR (C41-C43), and ICI blocks PM DOR allowing isolation of IC DOR signaling (C44-C47). PTX experiments (C48-C49) rule out competition with endogenous G proteins as explanation for miniGsi absence.

result: Immunofluorescence microscopy confirms that Nb39, but not miniGsi, is recruited to intracellular DOR specifically localized to the Golgi (colocalization with TGN-38 marker). Treatment with CNA (to block PM DOR) plus SNC80 significantly increases Nb39 Golgi enrichment but not miniGsi enrichment.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by fixed-cell immunofluorescence data (Figures 2D-G) using the Golgi marker TGN-38. Statistical analysis shows significant Nb39 enrichment (p<0.0001, Figure 2F) but not miniGsi (p=0.0654, Figure 2G). This confirms the live-cell imaging results and establishes the Golgi as the specific intracellular compartment.

result: β-arrestin-1 and β-arrestin-2 are recruited to PM DOR upon SNC80 treatment but are not recruited to intracellular/Golgi DOR, similar to the miniGsi pattern. This indicates that β-arrestins interact only with agonist-activated DOR at the plasma membrane.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by both confocal and TIR-FM imaging data (Figures 3A-F). The absence of intracellular recruitment is clearly demonstrated (Figure 3C, no significant increase), while PM recruitment is visible and quantifiable (Figures 3D-F). This parallel with miniGsi strengthens the conclusion about location-specific effector coupling.

result: Golgi-localized DOR is competent to inhibit forskolin-stimulated cAMP production. When PM DOR is blocked with ICI, SNC80 (membrane-permeable) still decreases cAMP in cells with intracellular DOR, but DPDPE (membrane-impermeable) does not. Intracellular DOR activation suppresses cAMP to approximately half the level of combined PM and IC DOR activation.
evaluation: Claims C62-C70 are well-supported by FRET-based cAMP measurements (Figures 4A-J, Figure 4-supplement 1). The experimental design properly isolates IC DOR contribution using ICI blockade and CHX treatment. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.0001, Figures 4I-J). The DPDPE control (C70) confirms specificity. The quantitative comparison (C67) is clearly shown in the data.

result: The main conclusion: DOR at the Golgi and plasma membrane both inhibit cAMP but engage distinct conformational biosensors and effectors in response to the same ligand. The local subcellular environment determines the active conformational states that receptors adopt, allowing GPCRs to couple to different effectors at different locations.
evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C12-C14, C71-C72 represent the integrated conclusions supported by the collective experimental evidence. The differential biosensor recruitment (Nb39 vs miniGsi), differential β-arrestin recruitment, and maintained cAMP inhibition at both locations together strongly support the conclusion that subcellular location determines conformational landscapes and effector coupling. This is the central finding of the manuscript.

result: Background context establishing the prevailing model of GPCR activation, the role of β-arrestins, challenges in biased agonist development, and prior work on DOR localization and biosensor characterization in related opioid receptors.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C11, C15-C19 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study. The citations appear appropriate and the claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field.

result: Methodological details: PC12 cells treated with NGF retain newly synthesized DOR in intracellular compartments. Cells were cultured, transfected, and labeled using standard protocols with specific reagents and conditions detailed for reproducibility.
evaluation: Claims C31, C90-C94 describe experimental methods. C31 is supported by citations to prior work (Kim and von Zastrow, 2003; Shiwarski et al., 2017a) and imaging data (Figures 1H-I). The other claims are straightforward methodological descriptions that are standard and appropriately detailed.

result: Discussion context: Prior structural and functional studies of opioid receptors, biosensors, and related GPCRs; potential mechanisms for location-dependent conformational differences including lipid composition, pH, sodium concentration, and receptor-interacting proteins; comparison with other GPCRs (B1AR, A1-adenosine receptor) showing different location-dependent behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C55-C57, C61, C73-C87 are discussion points supported by appropriate citations. These provide mechanistic context and compare findings to other systems. The citations appear accurate and the speculative elements (C72, C78, C83) are appropriately qualified. C86 makes a valid inference from cited work about miniGsi capability in Golgi.
